title: CORS Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Quick revision notes on how browsers enforce the same-origin policy and how CORS relaxes it: simple vs preflighted requests, Access-Control-Allow-* headers, credentials and wildcard rules, preflight caching, and the mistakes that break real apps.

chapters.title: Same-Origin Policy and the CORS Mental Model
points: Origin = scheme + host + port; any one differing makes a request cross-origin (https://a.com vs http://a.com, a.com vs api.a.com, :3000 vs :4000)
Same-origin policy blocks JS from READING cross-origin responses; the request is often still sent and executed by the server
CORS is a browser-enforced opt-in: the server declares who may read its responses via headers; curl, Postman and servers ignore CORS entirely
CORS is not server security or auth: it protects users' browsers, so it cannot stop attackers calling your API directly
Browser attaches an Origin request header on cross-origin requests; the server's response must allow it or the browser hides the response and logs a CORS error

chapters.title: Simple vs Preflighted Requests
points: Simple request: method GET, HEAD or POST only, no custom headers, and Content-Type limited to text/plain, multipart/form-data or application/x-www-form-urlencoded; sent directly, then response checked
Anything else is preflighted: PUT, PATCH, DELETE, custom headers like Authorization or X-Api-Key, or Content-Type: application/json
Preflight is an automatic OPTIONS request carrying Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers; the real request is sent only if it passes
Preflight response must be 2xx (200 or 204) with matching Allow headers; the browser sends no cookies on the preflight and it never reaches your route auth
Example: fetch(url, {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body}) triggers OPTIONS first, then POST; the same call with text/plain would be simple

chapters.title: Access-Control-Allow-* Response Headers
points: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: one exact origin or *; the browser compares it to the request Origin, and multiple comma-separated origins are invalid
Access-Control-Allow-Methods (preflight response): lists permitted methods, e.g. GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers (preflight response): must cover every name in Access-Control-Request-Headers, e.g. Content-Type, Authorization

Access-Control-Expose-Headers: by default JS reads only CORS-safelisted response headers (Cache-Control, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Type, Expires, Last-Modified, Pragma); list others like X-Total-Count here
Allowing several origins: check Origin against an allowlist, echo it back in Allow-Origin, and add Vary: Origin so caches do not serve the wrong origin's response

chapters.title: Credentials, Wildcards and Preflight Caching
points: Cookies and HTTP auth cross-origin need both sides: client credentials:'include' (fetch) or withCredentials=true (XHR), and server Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
With credentials, Allow-Origin cannot be *; it must be the exact origin, and Allow-Methods/Allow-Headers/Expose-Headers also cannot be * (wildcard is literal)
Bearer tokens in the Authorization header are not 'credentials' mode, but Authorization still forces a preflight and must be listed in Allow-Headers; * does not cover Authorization
Access-Control-Max-Age: N caches the preflight result for N seconds per origin+URL; Chrome caps at 7200s (2h), Firefox at 86400s (24h), default is 5s

Cached preflight skips repeat OPTIONS calls (saves a round trip per request); a permission removed on the server keeps working until the cache expires, while a method or header missing from the cache triggers a fresh preflight

chapters.title: Common CORS Mistakes and Debugging
points: Setting CORS headers only on success: error responses (401, 404, 500) lacking Allow-Origin show up as a misleading CORS error that hides the real status
Not handling OPTIONS: auth middleware or routing returns 401/404/405 on the preflight; answer OPTIONS before auth, with 2xx
Reflecting any Origin with Allow-Credentials: true lets any site read authenticated responses; always validate against an allowlist
Duplicate headers (proxy plus app both adding Allow-Origin) produce 'multiple values' errors; set CORS in exactly one layer

Redirects on preflight fail (preflight must not redirect); no-cors mode returns an opaque response you cannot read, so it is not a fix; debug via DevTools Network tab: check the OPTIONS request and response headers

chapters.title: CORS Cheat Sheet
points: Origin = scheme + host + port; the browser enforces, the server opts in via headers; non-browser clients ignore CORS
Simple: GET/HEAD/POST + safelisted headers + form or text content types; everything else (JSON, Authorization, PUT/DELETE) preflights via OPTIONS
Preflight request headers: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, Access-Control-Request-Headers; response: Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, Allow-Headers with 2xx
Credentials need client credentials:'include' plus Allow-Credentials: true and an exact Allow-Origin (no * anywhere); add Vary: Origin when echoing origins
Max-Age caches preflight (Chrome 2h cap, Firefox 24h); expose custom response headers with Expose-Headers; CORS errors often mask 4xx/5xx or an unhandled OPTIONS
